before: For references, == asks whether both refer to the same object. String.equals compares the characters in the two strings.

new String("Moon") creates a separate String object. Two such objects can contain equal text without being the same object. String literals may be shared internally, so do not generalize from literal identity comparisons.
Assigning second = first makes both variables refer to the same String object. It does not create a new object or change the text.

Expected output or behavior: false
true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare two explicitly new equal strings with two references to one string. Explain identity and equality separately. You may trace it without a JDK; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An object is a value with its own data and behavior. A reference points to an object. For String references, == checks whether both point to the same object. equals checks whether their text matches.
Each new String call here creates a separate object. Both objects can hold the same text. Use equals to compare String text; matching text alone does not tell you what == will return.
A String's text cannot be changed after the object is made. Text-changing methods return a result instead. Store that result if you want to use it later.
Assigning first to second copies the reference. Both variables then point to one String object. The assignment does not copy or change its text.
The program prints false, then true on the next line. The objects are separate, but their text matches.
The quiz replaces second's starting value with first. Decide how that changes which object second points to.

before.question: Replace second’s initializer with first. What do the two comparisons print?
choices: false then false because assigning references erases text.
true then true because both identity and text now match.
true then false because identity prevents equals from working.
before.explanation: Both variables now refer to one object, whose text is naturally equal to itself.

after.question: Use String second = first; instead. What do the comparisons print?
choices: false then false, because the text is erased.
true then true, because both variables point to the same String.
true then false, because equals cannot compare one object to itself.
after.explanation: Both variables point to one object, so == is true. That object's text also matches itself, so equals is true.
